A cadenza is a solo passage in a musical piece — usually a concerto — where one performer plays alone, without any accompaniment, to display their skill and artistry. Think of it as a spotlight moment. The rest of the orchestra goes completely silent, and for a stretch of time, the soloist has the stage entirely to themselves.

To understand a cadenza, you first need to know what a concerto is: a large piece of music for a solo instrument (like a violin, piano, or flute) and an orchestra, where the two take turns and interact throughout. A cadenza is the moment in a concerto where the orchestra stops, and the soloist performs alone.

It typically appears near the end of the first movement of a concerto — right before the final closing section. It feels like the movement is winding down, the orchestra plays a big, unresolved-sounding chord, and then — silence. The soloist enters.

During a cadenza, the soloist does several things at once:

  • Revisits themes from the movement — takes the melodies you've already heard and spins them into something new, more elaborate, or emotionally heightened.
  • Shows off technical mastery — cadenzas are often extremely difficult to play. They may involve blazing fast runs, wide leaps, complex rhythms, or multiple musical lines played simultaneously.
  • Plays freely — the performer is not locked into a strict, metered tempo. They can stretch time, linger on certain notes, rush forward, and breathe wherever they feel. This freedom gives the cadenza an improvisatory, spontaneous quality, even when it's been planned and rehearsed down to the last note.

The cadenza ends — almost always — with a trill (a rapid alternation between two adjacent notes). This trill is a musical signal to the orchestra: "I'm finishing up, get ready." The orchestra then re-enters to bring the movement to its close.

This is one of the most interesting things about the cadenza historically.

In the Baroque and early Classical periods (roughly the 1600s–1700s), cadenzas were improvised. The composer would leave a gap in the score — essentially a pause with an instruction — and the performer was expected to make something up on the spot, using their knowledge, creativity, and technical ability. This was considered a mark of a great musician.

Over time, as concert music became more structured and composers wanted more control over their work, cadenzas started being written out in full by the composer. Beethoven was a prominent figure in this shift — he sometimes even wrote explicit instructions forbidding the performer from improvising, and composed the cadenza himself. By the Romantic era (1800s), most cadenzas were written out.

This also created an interesting tradition: when a composer did not write a cadenza (as was common in earlier concertos), later performers and composers would write their own versions. As a result, a single famous concerto can have many different cadenzas, each reflecting a different performer's personality and musical ideas. For example, Beethoven's Violin Concerto has famous cadenzas written by performers like Fritz Kreisler and Joseph Joachim — none by Beethoven himself.

The cadenza also appears in opera, in vocal music. At the climax or end of an aria (a solo song for a singer), a singer might perform a cadenza — an elaborate, ornate flourish that shows off the range, agility, and beauty of their voice. In older opera, this too was improvised; singers would add their own decorations to show their vocal skill. In later opera, composers tended to write out these moments themselves.

If you were to listen to a concerto and had no idea what a cadenza was, you would still notice it immediately. The music is moving forward with the full orchestra, then suddenly the orchestra drops out, and one instrument bursts into a long, free, elaborate, often dazzling solo. It feels different from the rest of the piece — more personal, more daring, more unpredictable. It stands apart from the surrounding music almost the way a speech stands apart from a conversation.

Outside of music, "cadenza" is occasionally used in a figurative or informal sense to describe any moment of brilliant, virtuosic, or showy solo performance — in speech, in comedy, in writing, or in any art form. If a writer describes someone's monologue as "a verbal cadenza," they mean it was impressive, elaborate, and felt like a solo spotlight moment. This usage is less common, but you may encounter it in literary or arts writing.

AspectWhat it means

A cadenza is a solo spotlight moment in a concerto or opera, where the soloist plays or sings alone, without the orchestra, in a free and technically demanding passage. It shows off skill and expression, is usually placed near the end of a movement, ends with a trill that brings the orchestra back, and has evolved from something improvised to something mostly written out by composers. Outside of music, it can refer to any virtuosic solo performance in a broader sense.
